drills.q: Define one-way door vs two-way door decisions and how process should differ between them.
drills.a: Two-way door: cheap to reverse, decide fast at lowest competent level, minimal process. One-way door: expensive/impossible to reverse, decide slowly, get more input, document reasoning (ADR).

drills.q: Your team wants to write an ADR for every dependency version bump. Push back — why?
drills.a: It defeats the purpose: ADRs exist for architecturally significant, hard-to-reverse, or precedent-setting decisions. Writing one for everything drowns the signal and the practice eventually gets abandoned, taking the useful cases down with it.

drills.q: A scorecard shows your chosen database winning on all 6 criteria over both alternatives. Is this a good sign?
drills.a: No — it's a red flag that weights/scores were reverse-engineered to justify a pre-made decision. Real tradeoffs produce a mixed picture where the winner loses on 1-2 criteria but wins on the ones weighted most important.

drills.q: Why is swapping an LLM API provider often more of a one-way door than it looks?
drills.a: The API interface may be compatible, but fine-tuning data, prompts tuned to one provider's quirks, and an evaluation harness built around that provider's output distribution represent real sunk investment that doesn't transfer cleanly to a new provider.

drills.q: What single question determines whether to build or buy a capability?
drills.a: Does it touch revenue, retention, margin, or a defensible moat (differentiation)? If yes, build; if it's undifferentiated plumbing (auth, payments, email), buy.

drills.q: A colleague uses a generic 10-criterion checklist (scalability, cost, ease of use, community, docs...) for every tech decision. What's wrong with this?
drills.a: Generic criteria are ones every mature option scores 'fine' on, so the total is dominated by noise. Criteria should be derived from THIS decision's actual constraints (specific query pattern, team depth, scale number, consistency requirement).

drills.q: A new hire challenges a technology choice made 18 months ago in a design review. How do you respond without steamrolling or capitulating?
drills.a: Restate the original constraint (not just the decision), check the ADR if one exists, verify whether the constraint has actually changed since then. If unchanged, explain the original tradeoff, concede honestly where the alternative is genuinely better, and hold the conclusion if the original reasons still apply.

drills.q: You built an in-house AI eval harness in 2023 because no vendor existed. It's 2026 and vendors now exist. Do you switch?
drills.a: Not automatically — weigh the now-mature vendor's capability/cost against the switching cost (two years of tuning specific to your data) plus ongoing maintenance burden of the in-house system. This should have been a documented 'what would change this decision' trigger in the original ADR, checked periodically rather than assumed permanent.

drills.q: How would you design an AI system's model choice today to make it more genuinely reversible 18 months from now?
drills.a: Abstract the model call behind a provider-agnostic interface, keep the evaluation harness's golden set and rubrics provider-agnostic, and avoid encoding provider-specific prompt quirks where a more portable phrasing works — reversibility has to be deliberately engineered in, not assumed from having a REST API.

drills.q: A VP wants one technology-selection framework mandated across a 200-engineer org. What do you keep and what do you push back on?
drills.a: Keep: requiring a written ADR with alternatives-considered for architecturally significant/hard-to-reverse decisions, and classifying reversibility before debating options. Push back on: a single fixed criteria/weight list mandated org-wide, since criteria must be derived per-decision — enforce the ADR's structural shape at the org level, not the specific content.
